segment:
She smiled in a friendly way, but he didn’t respond. She thought for a second he was a statue and wondered why no one else seemed to have seen him yet.
Then his shoulders moved, subtly, in the direction of the couch. It seemed less like an invitation than a challenge.
Mara stopped in the middle of the room and looked around, at the empty chairs and tables, at the wall lined with books. She saw no place that looked more inviting than the couch, but she didn’t want to make him move or turn again if he didn’t want to. So she stood still.
He didn’t look away. She realized that he was going to wait her out, and decided to see who would blink first.
The pause stretched. The sound of voices rose faintly from somewhere outside the building. He leaned back further against the wall, and she could almost feel his muscles stretch and relax.
After what seemed like minutes, she felt a slight sensation in the back of her neck, as though someone were breathing there, or had laid a hand lightly against the nape of her neck.
She turned around, but nobody was there.
“I’m Mara,” she said aloud. “What’s your name?”
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

segment:
“Hi,” she said, going on in, “I’m Mara.”
He was a boy, younger than she had guessed, no more than a teenager.
He blinked and sat up to offer her his hand. “Welcome to Fulcrum. I’m Jonah.”
Mara shook his hand. It was pale and cool but not damp, the fingers smooth but firm.
“You’re one of the scientists, I take it?”
“No. I’m a subject.” His voice sounded slightly strained. “Like you.”
She blinked at him. “I thought most of the subjects here were adults. It sounded like that from the application materials.”
“Not all of them,” he said shortly. “You’re an adult, and I’m a boy. So there.”
“Well, I didn’t mean to sound like—”
A door opened behind her and she turned toward it. Adrian came in, wearing a plain black shirt with gray jeans and black dress shoes, and smiled at her. “Mara! So nice to meet you—and I see you’ve met Jonah already.” He shook his head. “So sorry we weren’t able to receive you on your arrival. Livia’s down with the flu, as it turns out. It must have been quite something to find yourself here with no one at hand to show you around.”

segment:
She thought it might be the boy with the dark hair she’d met in the hall last night, but he had brown eyes. She cleared her throat and said hi.
“Hi,” he echoed, without enthusiasm.
He shifted then to sit upright, legs uncrossed. The arm resting on the wall came down onto his thigh, fingers curled around his knee. Mara blinked, thinking at first that it was the angle of the light that made the hair on his wrist seem so fine and fair, but then she saw that his lower arms and legs were covered with what looked like down, fine golden hairs against his pale skin.
She’d read about hypertrichosis, though she’d never met anyone with it. She was pretty sure that this wasn’t the congenital kind, though—not with that one spot on his chest she’d seen last night, and not with the light color of the hair and the delicate curl and length to it.
“How come?” she asked.
He looked down at his legs in surprise, as if he hadn’t realized how he was sitting.
“Huh? Oh.” He let one hand rest on his knee and gave his arm a small pat with the other, as if it was a dog he’d called to his side. “Livia said I can’t do the training if I’m not taking the drugs. So I stopped.”

segment:
The floor felt like ice under her feet as she moved across it toward the sofa. He rose and made her a formal bow, then gestured to the seat he’d occupied. His eyes never left hers for an instant; she knew this had to be one of Livia’s men.
She took her place on the couch, aware that he was standing behind it. “Hi,” she said. “I’m Mara.” She glanced up at him, aware of the height difference and of the oddness of talking to someone who stood above her and didn’t offer to sit down.
“Jonah,” he said, his head nodding slightly. “I am Fulcrum.” His voice was deep and smooth.
Mara blinked at him; she hadn’t understood a word, though she knew that she’d heard correctly. “What?” she asked.
“Fulcrum is the name of this institute,” he explained. “We study communication here, all kinds of communication. It is also the name of what we do here. It is the name of my training and of Livia’s. I am Fulcrum.”
It all made perfect sense. She nodded, slowly. She could see no reason why he should offer to sit down. “And,” she added, “so is Livia. Or so she says.”

segment:
The lips might be smiling and might not. His eyes were dark enough that Mara couldn’t make out the shape of the iris.
Then he spoke in a clear voice. “I hope you didn’t wake me.”
That made it smile. Mara opened her mouth and closed it, not certain how to answer. After a moment, she said, “You’re Adrian, then?”
“I’m not your new partner,” the dark eyes clarified. “But I’m the other one.”
She was even less certain what this meant, but decided to take another stab anyway. “Who’s my partner?”
The blond head tipped a fraction to the right; that made the face into a profile and deepened Mara’s uncertainty. “You didn’t have one yet. But Jonah will be back soon.”
A pause lengthened between them. Adrian didn’t move again, and Mara wasn’t sure what to do with that. She cleared her throat before she could stop herself, and said, “What should I—”
A man’s footstep came through the door behind her, and her heart thumped harder. Was that Jonah? She turned toward him. The same dark hair as Adrian’s, the same narrow face but with a mustache that cut the space in two. The same casual stance in a blue-and-black robe, one palm raised in front of him.
A palmful of steaming green tea in a small cup.

Then he sat up and leaned forward, setting both feet on the floor and bracing one arm on the chairback behind him.
“Oh, great,” he said. “New person.”
She stood where she was for another beat, taking this in.
Then she walked straight across the room and offered her hand. “Hi.”
He stared at the offered hand for a second before standing, taking it, and shaking it firmly. She let him decide which way to go, and he pulled her to the couch beside him, sitting down. She sat beside him as they both waited, not looking at each other.
“Jonah.”
“Mara. I’m the new one,” she said. “I’m sorry; I didn’t know the party would be so late, or—”
“It isn’t a party,” he said, glancing up at her face. He didn’t look older than she’d thought from behind; maybe not even eighteen. But the face was very open as it searched hers, and she met his gaze. “We don’t have parties here. This isn’t that sort of place. You haven’t heard of us?”
“I heard your name, but—”
“Fulcrum. We’re Fulcrum.” He’d gone back to looking around the room as he spoke. Now he glanced at her again and she was reminded that he hadn’t really been listening either. She shrugged and looked away as he looked away, wondering who she’d talked with in the hallway.
